title: Refresh or Realize? Compute Allocation in Drifting Models

paper.title: Refresh or Realize? Compute Allocation in Drifting Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Drifting Models train a one-step generator by recomputing a finite-sample drift field at every
iteration and taking an optimizer step toward the drifted target. The field says how generated
samples should move, but the step is taken in parameters shared by all samples, so the motion the
network actually makes need not match the motion it was given. This leaves a basic training question
open: should extra compute go into fitting the current target more closely, or into recomputing the
field? We study it on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Holding the target fixed for k k optimizer steps and
measuring the realized displacement, we find that deeper fitting does bring the network closer to
the frozen target, and that the number of steps needed before it makes any net progress drops from
about sixteen early in training to one later on. When the extra steps come for free, k = 2 k=2 also
lowers FID. Once they are paid for, the result flips: at approximately matched measured wall-clock,
spending the budget on fresh fields gives lower FID than deeper fitting, on both training seeds. The
target itself shows why a fresh field is worth so much. Redrawing the finite support rotates its
direction far more than a parameter update does (cosine ≈ 0.3 \approx 0.3 – 0.6 0.6 against ≈ 0.95 \approx 0.95 ),
and a correction that is optimal in field space is not reliably better in FID than a
parameter-free one. For Drifting, fitting each target well and spending compute well are different
goals.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) train a one-step generator around a strikingly simple rule. A vector field V p , q V_{p,q} , computed from generated samples and real data, says how each generated sample should move so that the generated distribution q q drifts toward the data distribution p p , x i + 1 = x i + V p , q i ​ ( x i ) , x_{i+1}=x_{i}+V_{p,q_{i}}(x_{i}), (1) and training carries the rule out by freezing the drifted point x + V x+V as a regression target and taking an optimizer step toward it. Read this way, a training iteration moves samples along the field. Figure 1: A field can become easier to realize and still not be the best place to spend compute. (a) Drifting prescribes a motion V V toward a frozen target; one optimizer step executes a tangent-filtered motion Δ ​ H 1 ≈ η ​ K ​ V \Delta H_{1}\approx\eta KV that need not coincide with V V ; repeated steps against the same frozen target move closer (dotted: remaining residual). (b) Measured on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 at the state from which all our downstream runs start: net progress toward the frozen target grows with depth apart from a small dip at k = 2 k=2 . (c) With the number of refreshes fixed, k = 2 k=2 takes two optimizer steps per refresh and reaches lower FID on both training seeds. (d) At approximately matched measured wall-clock, k = 1 k=1 affords more refreshes and reaches lower FID on both seeds. Panels (c) and (d) share one FID axis. In practice the move is made in parameter space. The optimizer changes one set of weights shared by every sample in the batch, so all outputs move together, and to first order a single gradient step displaces the stacked outputs 𝐇 \mathbf{H} by Δ ​ 𝐇 1 = η ​ 𝐊𝐕 , 𝐊 = 𝐉𝐉 ⊤ , 𝐉 = ∂ 𝐇 / ∂ 𝜽 . \Delta\mathbf{H}_{1}=\eta\mathbf{K}\mathbf{V},\qquad\mathbf{K}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^{\top},\quad\mathbf{J}=\partial\mathbf{H}/\partial\bm{\theta}. (2) Sample i i thus moves by a mixture η ​ ∑ j 𝐊 i ​ j ​ 𝐕 j \eta\sum_{j}\mathbf{K}_{ij}\mathbf{V}_{j} of the motions prescribed for the whole batch rather than by its own 𝐕 i \mathbf{V}_{i} , and only in special geometries does η ​ 𝐊𝐕 \eta\mathbf{K}\mathbf{V} coincide with 𝐕 \mathbf{V} . In general the motion the field prescribes and the motion one step executes differ ( Fig. 1 a), and Eq. 1 is silent about the difference. This paper is about that difference: our object of study is the training loop that estimates the existing field from data and realizes it with an optimizer, rather than the definition of the field. The most direct way to study this gap is to remove the target as a variable. We freeze one target and take k k optimizer steps toward it instead of one; since the target cannot change, whatever happens to the executed motion is due to fitting alone. We use this frozen-target construction purely as a probe of realization. Measured on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 with an exact decomposition of the frozen-target residual ( Section 3 ), deeper fitting does close part of the gap ( Fig. 1 b), and closes it more readily as training proceeds: the depth at which fitting first makes net progress toward the target falls from about sixteen steps at checkpoint 5k to a single step by 20k. Whether that improvement is worth its cost is a separate question. Every Drifting iteration spends compute on two things: refreshing the field, by drawing a new finite support of real examples and building a new target, and realizing it with optimizer steps. Since deeper fitting demonstrably works, a case against it cannot rest on an optimizer that fails to fit. When the extra steps cost nothing, deeper fitting wins: at an equal number of refreshes, two steps per refresh reach lower FID than one on both training seeds ( Fig. 1 c). When the steps are paid for, the ordering reverses. At approximately matched measured wall-clock, the run that spends its budget on more refreshes, one step each, reaches lower FID on both seeds ( Fig. 1 d), although it used 9.8 % 9.8\% less time than its counterpart on one seed and 1.9 % 1.9\% more on the other. A local, matched-compute version of the same decision points the same way. Starting from a common parameter state, refreshing the target before the next update beats a second update toward the stale target in all 40 40 probes we ran, across three support sizes and three training stages. The same probes show where the value of refreshing comes from. At fixed parameters, a newly drawn support rotates the target direction far more (cosine 0.31 0.31 – 0.59 0.59 ) than one parameter update does at fixed support ( 0.94 0.94 – 0.98 0.98 ), so a second step against an old target keeps fitting one particular sample of a highly variable quantity, while a refresh replaces it. The size of that rotation is not a calibrated predictor of the local gain from refreshing, which stays nearly constant across support sizes that rotate the target by very different amounts ( Section 5 ). The target also depends strongly on how it is constructed. A same-budget correction to the target, calibrated by a held-out audit that follows a clean N − 1 / 2 N^{-1/2} law, is not reliably better in FID than a parameter-free split average, and removing a nominal 10 − 6 10^{-6} floor from the production affinity changes the aggregated field by 12 % 12\% . These measurements describe how the empirical field, its finite support and shared neural optimization interact inside the Drifting training loop. The executed motion is a tangent-filtered version of the prescribed one; how much of the prescription is carried out depends on realization depth, training state and batch geometry; executing a given target better is not the same as spending compute better; and the target itself is governed by its finite support and by implementation details. Refresh frequency, realization depth, support construction and affinity design are separate design axes of Drifting training, which Eq. 1 folds into a single notion of more optimization. Our contributions are: 1. an exact decomposition of frozen-target progress into aligned gain and orthogonal penalty, which makes the realization gap of Drifting measurable, and the finding on ImageNet that deeper fitting closes it, increasingly so over training; 2. the refresh–realize reversal: extra fitting lowers FID when it is free, whereas under approximately matched measured wall-clock refreshing wins on both training seeds and in all 40 40 local matched-compute probes; 3. evidence that support refresh, rather than the parameter update, dominates how the empirical target changes between steps; that field-space optimality of the target does not reliably transfer to FID; and that a nominal affinity floor materially changes the production field.

sections.heading: 4 Refresh or Realize? The Reversal
sections.text: Section 3 shows that extra optimization against a frozen target realizes it better. Training poses a different question: under a fixed budget, is that optimization better spent realizing the current field more accurately or obtaining a fresh one? We compare k = 1 k=1 and k = 2 k=2 optimizer steps per refresh for latent Drifting on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 at high positive support, with EMA weights, CFG 2.0 2.0 and 50k-sample FID, on two independently trained seeds. Wall-clock is the scheduler-reported elapsed time of each run. budget seed k = 1 k=1 k = 2 k=2 better equal refresh count k = 2 k{=}2 gets 2 × 2\times updates 42 7.56 7.26 k = 2 k=2 43 7.60 7.30 k = 2 k=2 ≈ \approx matched measured wall-clock 42 6.98 (32.2 h) 7.26 (35.7 h) k = 1 k=1 43 6.93 (34.5 h) 7.30 (33.9 h) k = 1 k=1 At an equal number of refreshes, k = 2 k=2 receives twice the optimizer updates and reaches lower FID on both seeds ( Table 2 , top). Deeper realization is therefore not a worse procedure, and the comparison rules out the explanation that k = 2 k=2 simply optimizes badly. Charging for the extra updates changes the outcome. At approximately matched measured wall-clock the k = 1 k=1 arm runs 45,252 45{,}252 refreshes and optimizer updates, against 30,000 30{,}000 refreshes and 60,000 60{,}000 updates for k = 2 k=2 , and it reaches lower FID on both seeds ( Table 2 , bottom): Under approximately matched measured wall-clock, refreshing the field outperforms deeper realization of the stale field in both training seeds. The two arms are matched only approximately, and the residual mismatch runs in opposite directions: on seed 42 the k = 1 k=1 run used 9.8 % 9.8\% less time, on seed 43 1.9 % 1.9\% more, while the FID ordering is the same in both. Run lengths were fixed from an estimated per-step cost before training. The same allocation decision, isolated at frozen checkpoints with matched compute and no scheduling effects, favors refreshing in all 40 40 probes we ran; Section 5 presents those probes together with what they reveal about the target. The operational consequence for this ImageNet regime is direct: when one and two optimizer steps per refresh are compared at approximately matched measured wall-clock, refreshing more often is the better allocation than a second step toward the same stale target. This is not an ordering over arbitrary depths, and we do not claim it for every field construction.

sections.heading: 5.1 Support refresh rotates the target, and the local decision favors it
sections.text: Between consecutive steps the parameters move and the support is redrawn. We separate the two at frozen checkpoints. From a state θ 0 \theta_{0} and target T 0 T_{0} we take one update to θ 1 \theta_{1} , then rebuild the target at θ 1 \theta_{1} twice: once from the same support ( T 1 same T_{1}^{\mathrm{same}} ) and once from a disjoint, freshly drawn support ( T 1 new T_{1}^{\mathrm{new}} ), with labels, generator noise and guidance draws held fixed. The same probe then makes the allocation decision with matched compute: realize takes a second update toward the stale T 0 T_{0} , refresh takes it toward T 1 new T_{1}^{\mathrm{new}} , and both are scored on two held-out supports that neither branch used. We ran eight probes in each of five cells, covering support sizes N ∈ { 64,128,256 } N\in\{64,128,256\} at checkpoint 30 30 k and training stages 10 10 k, 20 20 k and 30 30 k at N = 256 N=256 ( Appendix F ). The first three positions vary the support size at checkpoint 30k; the last three vary the training stage at N = 256 N=256 , sharing the N = 256 N=256 , 30k condition. (a) Cosine between the old target and the target rebuilt after one update, from the same support (dots) or a freshly drawn one (triangles); lines pair the two for each probe. (b) Held-out loss reduction of refresh over realize at matched compute; every probe is positive. Probes within a cell share a model state and are not independent. Figure 3 a shows the first result. Rebuilding the target from the same support after one update leaves its direction nearly unchanged (cosine 0.94 0.94 – 0.98 0.98 , mean 0.97 0.97 ); drawing a new support rotates it substantially (cosine 0.31 0.31 – 0.59 0.59 , mean 0.48 0.48 ), and more so the smaller the support. In the measured regime, resampling the finite support changes the target direction far more than the local parameter update itself. In these probes staleness is dominated by support resampling: a frozen target encodes one draw of a quantity that varies strongly from draw to draw, while one parameter update barely moves it. Figure 3 b shows the decision. Refreshing gives the lower held-out loss in all 40 40 probes, by 0.30 % 0.30\% to 1.49 % 1.49\% (median 0.56 % 0.56\% ). The probes share model states and support pools within a cell, so we read this as a consistent effect across varied conditions rather than as 40 40 independent trials. The two panels also separate two things that are easy to conflate. At checkpoint 30 30 k, the target rotates far more for N = 64 N=64 than for N = 256 N=256 , yet the mean refresh gain is almost identical ( 0.47 % 0.47\% and 0.48 % 0.48\% ); across training stages at N = 256 N=256 the rotation barely changes while the gain falls from 1.32 % 1.32\% at 10 10 k to 0.48 % 0.48\% at 30 30 k. Support sensitivity explains why refreshing changes the target; its magnitude is not a calibrated predictor of how much a refresh is worth.

sections.heading: 5.2 Field-space optimality does not reliably transfer to FID
sections.text: If the support dominates the target, a natural response is to spend part of each refresh improving the estimate. In this ImageNet audit β ∗ \beta^{\ast} follows an approximately N − 1 / 2 N^{-1/2} law, with fitted exponent − 0.50 -0.50 ( R 2 = 0.996 R^{2}=0.996 ) at checkpoint 30 30 k and − 0.47 -0.47 at 60 60 k ( Fig. 4 a). Figure 4: A clean law in field space does not become a reliable gain in FID. (a) The audit-optimal coefficient follows an approximately N − 1 / 2 N^{-1/2} law, stable between checkpoints 30 30 k and 60 60 k. (b) Downstream, the calibrated coefficient is not reliably better than the parameter-free β = 1 \beta=1 : it is better in three cells and worse in one, and the mean difference is − 0.005 -0.005 FID. Averaged over three evaluation seeds, the calibrated correction lowers FID in all six seed–support cells, by 0.040 0.040 on average, but only 13 13 of 18 18 individual paired evaluations are favorable, so the effect is comparable to evaluation noise. More to the point, the audit-optimal coefficient does not reliably outperform the parameter-free split average ( Fig. 4 b): a correction that is optimal in field space is not reliably optimal for downstream FID. We had also preregistered that the benefit would shrink as N N grows. The single-evaluation-seed results falsified this; averaging over evaluation seeds restores the predicted ordering, which we report as exploratory.

sections.heading: 5.3 A nominal affinity floor materially changes the production field
sections.text: The production field symmetrizes each affinity as max ⁡ ( p i ​ j row ​ p i ​ j col , 10 − 6 ) \sqrt{\max(p^{\mathrm{row}}_{ij}p^{\mathrm{col}}_{ij},\,10^{-6})} before forming the attraction and repulsion coefficients. The floor looks like a numerical safeguard, but at checkpoint 30 30 k it binds on about half of the τ = 0.05 \tau=0.05 affinities and on 91 % 91\% of the τ = 0.02 \tau=0.02 affinities. We recomputed the field with and without it, holding the checkpoint, labels, generator noise, guidance draws, generated features, supports and block weights identical, with a correctness gate against the compiled production code and a materiality threshold fixed before the run ( Appendix G ). Removing only the floor changes the aggregated production field by 12.3 % 12.3\% relative L 2 L_{2} (cosine 0.992 0.992 ); the τ = 0.05 \tau=0.05 and τ = 0.02 \tau=0.02 branches change by 10.8 % 10.8\% and 21.3 % 21.3\% . Because each temperature branch is RMS-normalized, every branch keeps its norm, so the floor acts on the direction of the field rather than its scale. The field Drifting optimizes in this regime includes the floor, and our conclusions describe that production field.

sections.heading: 6 Related Work
sections.text: Drifting ( Deng et al., 2026 ) arrived with a strong empirical result and comparatively little theory, and most follow-up work has been about the field itself. It has been read as a long–short flow map ( Li & Zhu, 2026 ) , as a Wasserstein gradient flow of a kernel-smoothed divergence ( Cao et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ) , and as score matching between kernel-smoothed distributions ( Turan & Ovsjanikov, 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) ; other work changes the field, replacing its displacement direction by kernel gradients ( Esteban-Casadevall et al., 2026 ) or adding momentum to counter spectral bias ( Brown et al., 2026 ) . These papers analyze the prescribed dynamics. Our object is the training loop that implements them: how much of the prescribed motion a shared network carries out, and how compute should be split between rebuilding the field and fitting it. A better-founded field still has to be estimated from a finite support and realized by an optimizer, so the two lines of work are complementary. Drifting is one of several routes to one- or few-step generation, alongside flow matching and rectified flow ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) and shortcut models ( Frans et al., 2025 ) , usually on transformer backbones ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) . What sets it apart for our purposes is that its regression target is rebuilt from data at every step, which is why a refresh–realize trade-off exists at all. The mechanism of Proposition 1 , a parameter update acting on outputs through 𝐊 = 𝐉𝐉 ⊤ \mathbf{K}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^{\top} , is the starting point of the neural tangent kernel literature ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ; Adlam & Pennington, 2020 ; Novak et al., 2022 ) , which has also been used to study adversarial generative training ( Franceschi et al., 2022 ) ; the frozen-target iteration of Proposition 2 is Landweber iteration ( Landweber, 1951 ; Engl et al., 1996 ) . We use this machinery to pose the realization question rather than to answer it, since our measurements are taken under AdamW, where the fixed-kernel model holds only approximately. The refresh–realize question also connects to two older ideas. Deep reinforcement learning deliberately holds regression targets fixed, refreshing target networks only periodically for stability ( Mnih et al., 2015 ) ; Drifting sits at the other end, because its target is a finite-sample estimate and a stale target mostly encodes the particular support it was built from. And, as with minibatch estimates of kernel discrepancies such as MMD ( Gretton et al., 2012 ) , the empirical Drifting target depends on the composition of its sample; we measure that dependence at the level of the direction a training step is asked to fit.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: The ImageNet evidence comes from two independently trained source seeds of latent Drifting at 256 × 256 256\times 256 , reported individually. The reversal rests on agreement across evidence rather than on seed count: both seeds order the arms the same way, the residual wall-clock mismatch changes sign between them, and the local probes agree. The long-run comparison tests one against two optimizer steps per refresh at approximately matched measured wall-clock; it does not establish an ordering over arbitrary depths or under exact compute matching. The support-size law for β ∗ \beta^{\ast} is fitted against a finite large-support reference and describes that audit rather than a population field. The comparisons are made on the production field, affinity floor included, and whether other affinity constructions shift the balance between refreshing and realizing remains open.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: Drifting prescribes a motion for every generated sample and leaves its execution to a shared network optimizer. We measured the gap between the two and what it implies for how training compute should be spent. Fitting a frozen target for longer does move the network closer to it, more so as training progresses, and with free extra steps it improves FID. Under approximately matched measured wall-clock the budget is nonetheless better spent recomputing the field, on both training seeds and in every local probe. Much of the explanation sits in the target: at fixed parameters, a new finite support changes its direction far more than an optimizer step does, and calibrating that target in field space does not carry over reliably to FID. Refresh frequency, realization depth and support construction are therefore design choices of the Drifting training loop in their own right, and the realization diagnostic introduced here measures the first two directly.

sections.text: All ImageNet results use the public JAX release of Deng et al. sections.heading: D.2 Realization depth without hidden confounders
sections.text: For k > 1 k>1 the frozen target must be recomputed from the parameters at the start of the outer iteration, never from the parameters as they move within it; our implementation rematerializes the target from the captured outer parameters for every micro-step after the first. Exponential moving average is updated once per outer iteration for every k k , so arms compared at a fixed outer horizon receive the same number of EMA updates. Weight decay is applied per micro-step at the rate that makes the per-outer decay identical across k k , i.e. ( 1 − η ​ λ inner ) k = 1 − η ​ λ outer (1-\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{inner}})^{k}=1-\eta\lambda_{\mathrm{outer}} . Without these three controls a k k comparison silently changes target staleness, averaging horizon and regularization at the same time.

sections.heading: D.3 Resource-matched protocol
sections.text: Two budget definitions appear in Section 4 . Equal outer iterations fixes the number of refreshes and lets k k determine the number of optimizer updates; this favors larger k k , and we report it first. Approximately matched measured wall-clock fixes the scheduler elapsed time; run lengths were set from an estimated per-step cost before the runs and the realized elapsed times are reported as measured, not as targets. We report both, together with optimizer-update counts, because ranking by outer iterations, by micro-steps, by FLOPs and by wall-clock can disagree ( Fig. 5 ).

sections.heading: D.4 Deterministic paired protocol for field-correction comparisons
sections.text: Every β \beta comparison in Section 5 is run as a matched pair: the two arms restore the same full training state, including optimizer moments and EMA, and are seeded per step before the data iterator and the memory-bank draw, so the two runs see identical batches, identical generator noise and identical support draws. The only difference between the arms is β \beta . Each arm’s positive support is drawn from a per-class bank whose size is twice the support size, and bank occupancy is asserted to exceed the support size at the first scientific update so that sampling never silently falls back to sampling with replacement.

Compute Allocation in Drifting Models Sipeng Chen Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Florida State University Email: sc25bg@fsu.edu Xu Zheng Affiliation: Knight Foundation School of Computing Affiliation: and Information Sciences Affiliation: Florida International University Email: xzhen019@fiu.edu Shibo Li Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Florida State University Email: sl24bp@fsu.edu Abstract Drifting Models train a one-step generator by recomputing a finite-sample drift field at every iteration and taking an optimizer step toward the drifted target. The field says how generated samples should move, but the step is taken in parameters shared by all samples, so the motion the network actually makes need not match the motion it was given. This leaves a basic training question open: should extra compute go into fitting the current target more closely, or into recomputing the field? We study it on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Holding the target fixed for k k optimizer steps and measuring the realized displacement, we find that deeper fitting does bring the network closer to the frozen target, and that the number of steps needed before it makes any net progress drops from about sixteen early in training to one later on. When the extra steps come for free, k = 2 k=2 also lowers FID. Once they are paid for, the result flips: at approximately matched measured wall-clock, spending the budget on fresh fields gives lower FID than deeper fitting, on both training seeds. The target itself shows why a fresh field is worth so much. Redrawing the finite support rotates its direction far more than a parameter update does (cosine ≈ 0.3 \approx 0.3 – 0.6 0.6 against ≈ 0.95 \approx 0.95 ), and a correction that is optimal in field space is not reliably better in FID than a parameter-free one. For Drifting, fitting each target well and spending compute well are different goals. 1 Introduction Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) train a one-step generator around a strikingly simple rule. A vector field V p , q V_{p,q} , computed from generated samples and real data, says how each generated sample should move so that the generated distribution q q drifts toward the data distribution p p , x i + 1 = x i + V p , q i ​ ( x i ) , x_{i+1}=x_{i}+V_{p,q_{i}}(x_{i}), (1) and training carries the rule out by freezing the drifted point x + V x+V as a regression target and taking an optimizer step toward it. Read this way, a training iteration moves samples along the field. Figure 1: A field can become easier to realize and still not be the best place to spend compute. (a) Drifting prescribes a motion V V toward a frozen target; one optimizer step executes a tangent-filtered motion Δ ​ H 1 ≈ η ​ K ​ V \Delta H_{1}\approx\eta KV that need not coincide with V V ; repeated steps against the same frozen target move closer (dotted: remaining residual). (b) Measured on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 at the state from which all our downstream runs start: net progress toward the frozen target grows with depth apart from a small dip at k = 2 k=2 . (c) With the number of refreshes fixed, k = 2 k=2 takes two optimizer steps per refresh and reaches lower FID on both training seeds. (d) At approximately matched measured wall-clock, k = 1 k=1 affords more refreshes and reaches lower FID on both seeds. Panels (c) and (d) share one FID axis. In practice the move is made in parameter space. The optimizer changes one set of weights shared by every sample in the batch, so all outputs move together, and to first order a single gradient step displaces the stacked outputs 𝐇 \mathbf{H} by Δ ​ 𝐇 1 = η ​ 𝐊𝐕 , 𝐊 = 𝐉𝐉 ⊤ , 𝐉 = ∂ 𝐇 / ∂ 𝜽 . \Delta\mathbf{H}_{1}=\eta\mathbf{K}\mathbf{V},\qquad\mathbf{K}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^{\top},\quad\mathbf{J}=\partial\mathbf{H}/\partial\bm{\theta}. (2) Sample i i thus moves by a mixture η ​ ∑ j 𝐊 i ​ j ​ 𝐕 j \eta\sum_{j}\mathbf{K}_{ij}\mathbf{V}_{j} of the motions prescribed for the whole batch rather than by its own 𝐕 i \mathbf{V}_{i} , and only in special geometries does η ​ 𝐊𝐕 \eta\mathbf{K}\mathbf{V} coincide with 𝐕 \mathbf{V} . In general the motion the field prescribes and the motion one step executes differ ( Fig. 1 a), and Eq. 1 is silent about the difference. This paper is about that difference: our object of study is the training loop that estimates the existing field from data and realizes it with an optimizer, rather than the definition of the field. The most direct way to study this gap is to remove the target as a variable. We freeze one target and take k k optimizer steps toward it instead of one; since the target cannot change, whatever happens to the executed motion is due to fitting alone. We use this frozen-target construction purely as a probe of realization. Measured on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 with an exact decomposition of the frozen-target residual ( Section 3 ), deeper fitting does close part of the gap ( Fig. 1 b), and closes it more readily as training proceeds: the depth at which fitting first makes net progress toward the target falls from about sixteen steps at checkpoint 5k to a single step by 20k. Whether that improvement is worth its cost is a separate question. Every Drifting iteration spends compute on two things: refreshing the field, by drawing a new finite support of real examples and building a new target, and realizing it with optimizer steps. Since deeper fitting demonstrably works, a case against it cannot rest on an optimizer that fails to fit. When the extra steps cost nothing, deeper fitting wins: at an equal number of refreshes, two steps per refresh reach lower FID than one on both training seeds ( Fig. 1 c). When the steps are paid for, the ordering reverses. At approximately matched measured wall-clock, the run that spends its budget on more refreshes, one step each, reaches lower FID on both seeds ( Fig. 1 d), although it used 9.8 % 9.8\% less time than its counterpart on one seed and 1.9 % 1.9\% more on the other. A local, matched-compute version of the same decision points the same way. Starting from a common parameter state, refreshing the target before the next update beats a second update toward the stale target in all 40 40 probes we ran, across three support sizes and three training stages. The same probes show where the value of refreshing comes from. At fixed parameters, a newly drawn support rotates the target direction far more (cosine 0.31 0.31 – 0.59 0.59 ) than one parameter update does at fixed support ( 0.94 0.94 – 0.98 0.98 ), so a second step against an old target keeps fitting one particular sample of a highly variable quantity, while a refresh replaces it. The size of that rotation is not a calibrated predictor of the local gain from refreshing, which stays nearly constant across support sizes that rotate the target by very different amounts ( Section 5 ). The target also depends strongly on how it is constructed. A same-budget correction to the target, calibrated by a held-out audit that follows a clean N − 1 / 2 N^{-1/2} law, is not reliably better in FID than a parameter-free split average, and removing a nominal 10 − 6 10^{-6} floor from the production affinity changes the aggregated field by 12 % 12\% . These measurements describe how the empirical field, its finite support and shared neural optimization interact inside the Drifting training loop. The executed motion is a tangent-filtered version of the prescribed one; how much of the prescription is carried out depends on realization depth, training state and batch geometry; executing a given target better is not the same as spending compute better; and the target itself is governed by its finite support and by implementation details. Refresh frequency, realization depth, support construction and affinity design are separate design axes of Drifting training, which Eq. 1 folds into a single notion of more optimization. Our contributions are: 1. an exact decomposition of frozen-target progress into aligned gain and orthogonal penalty, which makes the realization gap of Drifting measurable, and the finding on ImageNet that deeper fitting closes it, increasingly so over training; 2. the refresh–realize reversal: extra fitting lowers FID when it is free, whereas under approximately matched measured wall-clock refreshing wins on both training seeds and in all 40 40 local matched-compute probes; 3. evidence that support refresh, rather than the parameter update, dominates how the empirical target changes between steps; that field-space optimality of the target does not reliably transfer to FID; and that a nominal affinity floor materially changes the production field. 2 Background: Drifting as Refresh and Realize Following Deng et al. It has been read as a long–short flow map ( Li & Zhu, 2026 ) , as a Wasserstein gradient flow of a kernel-smoothed divergence ( Cao et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ) , and as score matching between kernel-smoothed distributions ( Turan & Ovsjanikov, 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) ; other work changes the field, replacing its displacement direction by kernel gradients ( Esteban-Casadevall et al., 2026 ) or adding momentum to counter spectral bias ( Brown et al., 2026 ) . These papers analyze the prescribed dynamics. Our object is the training loop that implements them: how much of the prescribed motion a shared network carries out, and how compute should be split between rebuilding the field and fitting it. A better-founded field still has to be estimated from a finite support and realized by an optimizer, so the two lines of work are complementary. Drifting is one of several routes to one- or few-step generation, alongside flow matching and rectified flow ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) and shortcut models ( Frans et al., 2025 ) , usually on transformer backbones ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) . What sets it apart for our purposes is that its regression target is rebuilt from data at every step, which is why a refresh–realize trade-off exists at all. The mechanism of Proposition 1 , a parameter update acting on outputs through 𝐊 = 𝐉𝐉 ⊤ \mathbf{K}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^{\top} , is the starting point of the neural tangent kernel literature ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ; Adlam & Pennington, 2020 ; Novak et al., 2022 ) , which has also been used to study adversarial generative training ( Franceschi et al., 2022 ) ; the frozen-target iteration of Proposition 2 is Landweber iteration ( Landweber, 1951 ; Engl et al., 1996 ) . We use this machinery to pose the realization question rather than to answer it, since our measurements are taken under AdamW, where the fixed-kernel model holds only approximately. The refresh–realize question also connects to two older ideas. Deep reinforcement learning deliberately holds regression targets fixed, refreshing target networks only periodically for stability ( Mnih et al., 2015 ) ; Drifting sits at the other end, because its target is a finite-sample estimate and a stale target mostly encodes the particular support it was built from. And, as with minibatch estimates of kernel discrepancies such as MMD ( Gretton et al., 2012 ) , the empirical Drifting target depends on the composition of its sample; we measure that dependence at the level of the direction a training step is asked to fit. 7 Scope and Conclusion Scope. The ImageNet evidence comes from two independently trained source seeds of latent Drifting at 256 × 256 256\times 256 , reported individually. The reversal rests on agreement across evidence rather than on seed count: both seeds order the arms the same way, the residual wall-clock mismatch changes sign between them, and the local probes agree. The long-run comparison tests one against two optimizer steps per refresh at approximately matched measured wall-clock; it does not establish an ordering over arbitrary depths or under exact compute matching. The support-size law for β ∗ \beta^{\ast} is fitted against a finite large-support reference and describes that audit rather than a population field. The comparisons are made on the production field, affinity floor included, and whether other affinity constructions shift the balance between refreshing and realizing remains open. Conclusion. Drifting prescribes a motion for every generated sample and leaves its execution to a shared network optimizer. We measured the gap between the two and what it implies for how training compute should be spent. Fitting a frozen target for longer does move the network closer to it, more so as training progresses, and with free extra steps it improves FID. Under approximately matched measured wall-clock the budget is nonetheless better spent recomputing the field, on both training seeds and in every local probe. Much of the explanation sits in the target: at fixed parameters, a new finite support changes its direction far more than an optimizer step does, and calibrating that target in field space does not carry over reliably to FID. Refresh frequency, realization depth and support construction are therefore design choices of the Drifting training loop in their own right, and the realization diagnostic introduced here measures the first two directly.
